To mope means to feel sad, gloomy, and sorry for yourself — and to just sit with that feeling without doing anything about it. When someone mopes, they are not actively crying or dramatically upset. Instead, they go quiet, become sluggish, lose interest in things around them, and drift around in a fog of low spirits. Think of it as a passive, self-absorbed kind of sadness.

The key detail that makes "mope" different from simply "feeling sad" is this: a person who mopes tends to dwell in their unhappiness rather than try to move past it. They give in to the gloomy feeling and let it take over.
What It Looks Like in Real Life

Imagine someone who didn't get invited to a party. Instead of talking about it or distracting themselves, they spend the whole evening lying on the sofa, staring at the ceiling, giving one-word answers, and sighing heavily. They don't want to eat, they don't want to watch TV, they don't want to do anything. That person is moping.

Or picture a footballer who got dropped from the team. For the next three days, he wanders around the house with slumped shoulders, barely speaking, looking gloomy and lost in his own sad thoughts. He is moping.

You will very often see "mope" used with the word around (or sometimes about):

  • "She's been moping around the house all day."
  • "Stop moping around and go do something."

"Mope around" paints the picture of someone physically moving through a space — but slowly, aimlessly, and joylessly — as if their sadness has stolen their energy and purpose.
The Subtle Tone of the Word

This is important: "mope" carries a very slight sense of judgment. When someone tells you "stop moping," they are not just observing your sadness — they are gently (or sometimes not so gently) suggesting that you are wallowing in it a little too much, and that it's time to shake it off. The word implies that the sadness, while real, has perhaps gone on longer than necessary, or that the person is being a little self-pitying.

This does NOT mean the sadness isn't real or valid. It just means "mope" often gets used when an outsider feels the person could try to move on but is choosing not to.
How It Differs from Similar Words

English has several words for being sad and withdrawn, and they are NOT the same:

  • Sulk — You are unhappy and you are deliberately going silent to punish someone or make them feel guilty. There's an angry, almost strategic element to it. "He sulked because his mum refused to buy him the toy."
  • Brood — You are quietly and deeply thinking about something that is troubling you. It's more internal and intense, less about self-pity, more about serious thought. "She brooded over the difficult decision for hours."
  • Grieve — This is deep, serious sadness, usually over a significant loss like a death. It is far heavier and more dignified than moping.
  • Mope — You are sad and feeling sorry for yourself, and you're not doing anything productive about it. It's low-energy, passive, and somewhat self-absorbed. It's lighter than grief but more prolonged and aimless than a quick sulk.

"Mope" is an everyday, informal word. You would use it in casual conversation, not in a formal essay or legal document. It can be used with warmth ("Aw, don't mope — things will get better!") or with mild frustration ("You've been moping for a week, enough now.").

• mope — base form: "Don't mope."
  • mopes — third person singular: "He always mopes when things don't go his way."
  • moping — present participle (the most commonly seen form): "She's been moping all afternoon."
  • moped — past tense: "He moped for days after losing the match." (Note: "moped" also means a small motorised bicycle — context will always make it clear which meaning is intended.)
  • mopey / mopy — the adjective form: "Why are you so mopey today?"

To mope is to quietly sink into a sad, self-pitying, low-energy state — drifting through your day without purpose or joy, dwelling on your unhappiness instead of doing anything about it. It is softer than grief, more passive than sulking, and less intense than brooding. People mope after disappointments, rejections, failures, or losses. And the word carries a gentle hint that the person could snap out of it — if only they tried.
